exercises.prompt: You want to switch your machine from one stable Rust release to the next one that just came out. Which tool do you use?

options.label: `rustup`
options.feedback: Yes. `rustup update` downloads the newest stable compiler, standard library and Cargo, and can keep several toolchains side by side.

options.label: `cargo`
options.feedback: Not yet. Cargo builds projects and manages their dependencies, but it does not install new versions of itself or the compiler.

options.label: `rustc`
options.feedback: Not yet. `rustc` is the compiler; it compiles code but cannot replace itself with a newer version.

options.label: crates.io
options.feedback: Not yet. crates.io is the registry of libraries (crates) that Cargo downloads from, not a toolchain installer.

hints: One tool manages toolchains; another manages projects.
The installer you ran at the very beginning stays on your machine to manage updates.
exercises.solution: **rustup** is the toolchain manager: `rustup update` moves you to the newest stable release, and `rustup toolchain list` shows what is installed. Cargo builds projects, `rustc` compiles, and crates.io hosts libraries.

options.label: It compiles and runs the program in debug mode.
It checks that the code compiles (types, borrowing and all) without producing an executable.
options.feedback: Yes. It skips code generation, so it is the quickest way to find out whether your program compiles.

options.label: It builds an optimised release executable.
It runs the project's tests.
options.feedback: Not yet. Tests run with `cargo test`, which you will meet in a later lesson.

hints: Which step of compiling is the slow one, and which steps find your mistakes?
exercises.solution: `cargo check` runs the compiler's analysis (parsing, type checking, borrow checking) but stops before generating machine code, so it is much faster than a build. Editors run it on every save to underline errors as you type.

hints: `{n}` prints the variable `n`; the next `{}` takes the first argument after the string.
There is nothing between the two `{}` in the second line, so the numbers are printed next to each other.
exercises.solution: The first line prints `n` (7), a colon and `n * n` (49): `7:49`. The second prints 4 and then 10 with nothing between them: `410`. The third divides 10.0 by 4.0 (2.5) and prints it with one decimal place: `2.5`. So: `7:49`, `410`, `2.5`.

feedback.message: Not yet. `print!` does not end the line, so `b` and `c` share one line, finished by the empty `println!()`.
Not yet. Look at the last string: `\n` inside it is a newline character, so `d` and `e` are on separate lines.

hints: `print!` writes without a newline; `println!()` with no arguments writes only a newline.
`\n` inside a string literal is a newline.
exercises.solution:
The output is

```text
a
bc
d
e
```

four lines. `print!("b")` and `print!("c")` write on the same line, and `println!()` ends it. The last string contains a newline escape, so it prints as two lines.

exercises.prompt: Why can the compiler reject `println!("{greting}")` when `greting` is misspelled, before the program runs?

options.label: Because `println!` is a macro, expanded at compile time, and it checks the format string against the variables in scope.
options.feedback: Yes. The format string is parsed while compiling, so every placeholder must refer to something that exists.

options.label: Because Rust runs every program once while compiling it.
options.feedback: Not yet. The compiler does not run your program; it analyses it.

options.label: Because string literals in Rust cannot contain braces.
options.feedback: Not yet. They can; in a format string a literal brace is written doubled, `{{`.

options.label: It can't: the misspelling is only noticed when the line runs.
options.feedback: Not yet. That is how many interpreted languages behave, but here the error E0425 appears at compile time.

exercises.solution: `println!` is a macro. Macros are expanded during compilation, and this one parses the format string, so `{greting}` becomes a reference to a variable named `greting`. There is no such variable, so the compiler reports error E0425 and even suggests `greeting`.

exercises.prompt: Which statements about Rust **editions** are true? Choose all that apply.

options.label: The edition is chosen per package, in `Cargo.toml`.
options.feedback: Yes. `edition = "2024"` in the manifest sets it.

options.label: A crate in the 2021 edition can depend on a crate in the 2024 edition.
options.feedback: Yes. Editions are a per-crate setting and crates of different editions link together, so the ecosystem does not split.

options.label: A new edition ships with every six-week release.
options.feedback: Not yet. Releases come every six weeks; editions have come roughly every three years (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024).

options.label: Editions let the language make a few incompatible changes, such as reserving new keywords, without breaking existing code.
options.feedback: Yes. Old code keeps its old edition and keeps compiling.

hints: Think about why a language that promises not to break old code would need editions at all.
exercises.solution: Editions are an opt-in, per-package setting (`edition` in `Cargo.toml`) that lets Rust make small incompatible changes while old code keeps compiling with its old edition. Crates of different editions work together. Editions are rare (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024); the six-week cycle is for ordinary releases.
